title: Decision Trees
tagline: Flowchart-style questions that split your data into smaller groups until you can make a prediction.
what_it_is: A decision tree is a model that looks like a flow chart. You start at the top (root) and ask a question about one feature, like 'is age < 30?'. Depending on the answer, you go down one branch. At the next node, you ask another question. You keep going until you reach a leaf node that gives you a prediction. For regression, the leaf gives a number (average of training values in that leaf). For classification, it gives a class (majority vote). Trees are easy to draw and explain, even to non-experts.
key_points: Split the data based on feature values to make the groups as pure as possible (all same class for classification, low variance for regression).
Splitting criteria: Gini impurity or entropy for classification, variance reduction for regression.
Depth of tree controls complexity: shallow trees underfit, deep trees overfit.
Can handle both numerical and categorical features without scaling.
Feature importance can be extracted from how much each feature reduces impurity.
why_it_exists: Linear models assume a straight line relationship. But many real problems have interactions and non-linearities that a straight line cannot capture. A decision tree can model complex decision boundaries like 'if young and male and lives in city, then buy product; else not'. Trees exist because they are intuitive – humans naturally think in if-then-else rules. They are also non-parametric, meaning they can fit any shape if you let them grow deep enough.
what_it_measures: A decision tree measures impurity (how mixed the classes are) at each node. The goal is to choose splits that decrease impurity the most. For classification, common measures are Gini impurity: probability of misclassifying a random element if you guessed according to the class distribution. And entropy: the amount of disorder. For regression, the measure is variance. The tree also measures feature importance: total reduction in impurity from splits on that feature, averaged across all nodes.
intuition: Imagine you are trying to guess if someone will like a movie. You ask questions one by one. 'Do they like action movies?' If yes, go to the next question: 'Are they under 30?' If yes, guess 'Yes, they will like it'. If no to action, ask 'Do they like romance?' If yes, guess 'Maybe'. That is a decision tree. Each question splits the group into subgroups that are more similar to each other. The tree is built automatically by a computer that tries all possible questions and picks the one that makes the subgroups most pure.

when_to_use: When you need an interpretable model. A small tree (depth 3-5) can be explained to anyone.
When relationships are non-linear and have interactions. Trees handle those naturally.
When you have mixed data types (numbers and categories) and don't want to scale features.
As a building block for random forests and gradient boosting (much more powerful).
When you want feature importance scores to understand which inputs matter.
when_not_to_use: Do not use a single deep decision tree – it will overfit badly. Use a random forest or limit depth with pruning.
Do not use decision trees if you need smooth predictions. Trees give step functions, not smooth curves.
Do not use trees with very small datasets. The tree might be unstable (small changes in data change the tree a lot).
Do not use trees if your features have many categories (e.g., zip codes with 1000 levels). The tree will be biased toward high-cardinality features.
common_mistakes: Growing a tree to full depth and then being surprised by overfitting. Always prune or set max_depth.
Using feature importance from a single tree as a reliable ranking. It can be unstable. Use random forest for stable importance.

Forgetting that decision trees are greedy – they pick the best split at each node without looking ahead. A different sequence of splits might be better globally, but greedy is fast and works well enough.
Assuming the tree is 'correct' if it perfectly fits training data. That is overfitting, not correctness.
ds_usage: In scikit-learn: `from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, DecisionTreeRegressor`. Use `model = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=5, min_samples_leaf=10)` to prevent overfitting. Fit, then predict. Visualize tree with `export_graphviz` or `plot_tree`. Feature importances: `model.feature_importances_`. Tune hyperparameters like `max_depth`, `min_samples_split`, `min_samples_leaf` via cross-validation. For real work, use random forest or gradient boosting instead of a single tree.
